prose.summary: A content strategist decides what gets written before anyone writes it: which pages exist, what argument each one makes, and how a reader moves from one to the next. That's the line that separates the role from a copywriter, who is usually handed the brief and asked to execute it. The strategist owns the map; other people, sometimes the strategist too, fill in the roads.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks split into a few planning blocks and a longer stretch of production and review. You'll open an editorial calendar or a roadmap doc on Monday, look at what's due against a launch or a campaign, and reorder priorities depending on what sales or product just changed. A good chunk of the week goes into briefs: what the piece needs to argue, who it's for, what it should rank for if SEO is part of the mandate (it usually is, for about a third of postings). Then there's review, sitting with a draft from a freelancer or a copywriter and marking where the argument goes soft. The moment people wait for is publishing day on something that took months to line up, a pillar page or a launch narrative finally going live and the analytics dashboard starting to move. Roughly half the week is heads-down writing or editing, the rest is meetings: with product marketing, with sales on what collateral they're missing, with whoever owns the CMS.
prose.work_environment: This is desk work, almost entirely computer and calendar, which is part of why over a third of postings are remote: there's no equipment or physical presence the job requires. The bad weeks come from launch clustering, three product releases landing in the same month with content due for all of them, or from a CMS migration that nobody budgeted proper time for. Hours are standard outside of launch crunch, though sales enablement work can pull you into whatever timezone the deal is happening in. Most of the job is written communication (Slack, docs, comments on a draft) rather than live meetings, which suits people who think better with a keyboard than out loud.
prose.getting_in: Most postings ask for around five years of experience, and only a fifth waive or skip a degree requirement, so the standard path runs through a few years as a writer or marketer before the title changes. A bachelor's degree is listed in the large majority of postings, but the two employers who explicitly waive it care more about a body of published or gated work than the credential. The slow part isn't learning the skills, it's accumulating a portfolio that shows you can own a content plan end to end, not just execute one piece at a time. People stall at the jump from writer to strategist because that jump requires evidence of judgment (what to prioritize, what to kill) and most day-to-day writing work doesn't generate that evidence on its own. B2B experience specifically shows up in nearly half of postings, so time spent writing for a business audience rather than consumer content counts for more than it might seem.
prose.ladder: Early on you're responsible for individual pieces: a blog post, a landing page, an email sequence, each judged on its own. The first real step up is owning a content pillar or a channel, meaning you're accountable for how a whole category of content performs together, not just whether one draft was good. Past that, the ladder forks: one branch goes into managing writers and freelancers and owns headcount and process, the other stays hands-on and moves into a principal or lead strategist role that still touches drafts but sets direction across multiple teams. That fork tends to show up somewhere around the five to eight year mark, roughly when someone would otherwise be interviewing for their second or third strategist title.
prose.suits: People who come alive in this job like holding the whole shape of something in their head, the way twelve blog posts and three case studies and a nurture sequence add up to one argument about why a customer should switch. The good day is watching a piece you scoped six weeks ago move a metric you were tracking, not just seeing it look nice published. People who leave usually wanted to write more and manage less; they signed up thinking strategist meant better writing assignments and found it meant fewer of them, replaced by briefs, calendars, and defending priorities in a roadmap review. If what you want is to write well and be left alone to do it, copywriter is the honester title.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders think the job is mostly writing, but for a strategist at the mid-to-senior level the writing is often the smallest part of the week, most of it goes into deciding what should be written and defending that plan to product and sales. There's also an assumption that this is a soft, opinion-based role with no numbers attached, when in practice a fifth of postings ask for data analysis explicitly, and strategists who can't read their own dashboard lose arguments to the people who can.
prose.who_qualifies: Marketing managers carry over the most (roadmap thinking, cross-team negotiation, budget awareness) but often need to relearn how to write a usable brief rather than just approve one. SEO specialists and growth marketers bring the measurement instinct and channel knowledge that a lot of strategist roles now expect, though they sometimes need to build up narrative and editorial judgment. Copywriters have the opposite gap: strong drafting, less practice owning a plan across multiple pieces and stakeholders. None of these are a clean швon-ramp; expect six months to a year of overlap work before the title itself changes.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: None of this shows how much of the job is internal politics, convincing a product manager that the launch narrative needs another week, or talking sales out of a one-off asset that won't scale. It also can't capture how much a strategist's leverage depends on who they report to; the same title means very different amounts of actual decision-making power depending on whether content sits under marketing or under a founder directly.

steps.do: Write and publish for two to three years
steps.how: Work as a writer, copywriter, or marketing generalist somewhere that lets you own more than single assignments, ideally a B2B company where the content has to argue something rather than just describe a product. This is the stretch that takes longest and can't be shortcut; aim for at least a handful of pieces you can point to that moved a real number (traffic, signups, pipeline).

steps.do: Build one real content plan, not samples
steps.how: Take a product or topic and build a small content roadmap for it: three to five pieces that build on each other toward one outcome, with a stated goal for each. This is the artifact that proves strategic thinking rather than drafting ability, and it takes a few weeks if you do it seriously rather than as a resume filler.

steps.do: Get SEO and data literacy, not certification
steps.how: Learn to read a search console or analytics dashboard well enough to explain why a page underperformed, since over a third of postings name SEO directly and a fifth want data analysis. A few weeks of hands-on practice with a real site (yours or an employer's) beats any course certificate here.

steps.do: Apply to strategist roles at year four or five
steps.how: Start applying once you have roughly five years combined writing and planning experience, matching the median this role asks for, and lean on B2B or SaaS postings first since that's where content-marketing and product-marketing skills overlap most with what you've built. Expect the interview to include a case study or writing sample defense, not just a portfolio review.

steps.do: Take a lead role or specialize deliberately
steps.how: Once you're in the seat, decide within a year or two whether you want to manage a team (own headcount, process, hiring) or go deeper as a principal-level individual contributor who still writes and edits but sets direction across teams. This decision shapes the next five years more than any skill you'll pick up along the way.

prose.tools: The real gatekeepers are content-marketing platforms and SEO tools (Ahrefs, SEMrush, or similar) since SEO shows up in over a third of postings, plus whatever CMS the company runs on, usually WordPress or a headless system. Data analysis tools (GA4, a BI dashboard) matter enough to mention in interviews even where they're not named outright. LLM tools now show up in about a fifth of postings, mostly for drafting speed and outline generation rather than replacing the strategic work, and that share is likely to keep climbing rather than plateau.

industries.name: B2B SaaS
industries.note: The largest single employer of this title; content has to educate a buyer through a long sales cycle, so strategists here spend real time with sales on what closes deals, not just what ranks.

industries.name: Agencies
industries.note: You run strategy for several clients at once instead of one brand, which means faster context-switching and less depth on any single voice, but broader exposure to different industries in a shorter time.

industries.name: Consumer tech and product companies
industries.note: Content leans more toward brand voice and launch storytelling than lead generation, and the work often sits closer to product marketing than to sales.

industries.name: Financial and professional services
industries.note: Heavier compliance review on every piece and a slower publishing cadence, but the strategic work (what to say, to whom, in what order) matters just as much.

specializations.name: Sales enablement content
specializations.why: It shows up in nearly a fifth of postings and pays well because it sits directly next to revenue; strategists who can build content that closes deals, not just attracts traffic, are hard to find and easy to justify budget for.

specializations.name: Product marketing crossover
specializations.why: Over a quarter of postings ask for product-marketing skills alongside content strategy, and companies increasingly want one person who can write the launch narrative and the ongoing content plan instead of two separate hires.

specializations.name: SEO-led content strategy
specializations.why: With SEO named in over a third of postings, strategists who can own both the editorial plan and the technical search side (site structure, keyword clustering) command a distinct track from generalist strategists and often move faster into senior roles.

pros: You get to watch an idea travel from a single Slack message to a published piece to a number on a dashboard that someone in a leadership meeting mentions.
The work rewards pattern recognition across a whole content library, not just a single sentence, which suits people who like solving structure problems as much as writing ones.
Remote availability is real here (over a third of roles), so the job travels with you rather than tying you to one office or city.
The path in doesn't require a license or a fixed credential, so a strong portfolio and a track record of results can outweigh a missing degree at more employers than people expect.
cons: The writing share of the job shrinks as you move up, so if drafting is what you love, the promotion path can quietly take it away from you.
Priorities get reshuffled by whatever product or sales needs this quarter, so a plan you spent weeks building can get half-abandoned mid-execution.
Proving impact is genuinely harder here than in most marketing roles, since content's effect on revenue is usually indirect and takes months to show up cleanly.
B2B and SaaS dominate the hiring pool, so if you want to write for a consumer brand or a mission-driven org, the open roles are fewer and the search takes longer.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a content strategist
faq.a: Most postings ask for around five years of relevant experience, so the realistic timeline is two to three years as a writer or marketer followed by another year or two building the planning and roadmap experience strategist roles screen for. People with strong B2B or SEO backgrounds sometimes move faster because those skills overlap directly with what the role needs.

faq.q: do you need a degree to be a content strategist
faq.a: Most postings list a bachelor's degree as required, but a meaningful minority (about a fifth combined) waive it or only prefer it, especially when the candidate has a strong portfolio of published, results-driving work. What substitutes for the degree is evidence: pieces you can point to that moved traffic, signups, or pipeline.

Yes, over a third of postings are remote, which is high for a role that still involves regular cross-team meetings. The work is mostly writing, planning, and async review, which travels well, though roles heavy on sales enablement may expect more overlap with client or sales team hours.

faq.q: content strategist vs copywriter, what's the difference
faq.a: A copywriter is handed a brief and writes the piece; a content strategist decides what pieces should exist, why, and in what order, and often writes the briefs copywriters work from. The pay reflects it too: strategist salaries here run noticeably higher than the copywriter range, and the jump between the two roles is one of the most common transitions in this field.

The drafting part of the job is increasingly assisted by LLM tools, which already show up in about a fifth of postings, but the planning and prioritization work (what should exist, for whom, in what order) is exactly what those tools can't decide on their own. If anything, faster drafting raises the value of the person deciding what's worth drafting in the first place.
